title: Quantum advantage prediction in turbulent free-space quantum illumination
authors: Yu Tang, Beining Xia, Qianqian Liu, Cuihong Wen, Heng Fan, Jieci Wang
abstract: Quantum illumination offers a significant theoretical advantage for target detection in high background noise environments. However, its practical deployment in free-space channels is hindered by atmospheric turbulence. Stochastic fluctuations in atmospheric turbulence inevitably degrade the quantum signature, rendering the real-time evaluation of quantum advantage under such dynamic conditions a critical yet unresolved challenge. To circumvent the reliance on costly direct turbulence measurements, we propose a physics-driven framework that integrates Kolmogorov-Arnold networks directly bridge macroscopic meteorological observations with microscopic quantum channel dynamics. Trained on 105,120 samples from 12 climatically diverse sites and validated on 26,280 unseen samples from three extreme boundary conditions (arid continental, tropical maritime, high-altitude plateau), our approach establishes a physically consistent mapping from standard meteorological variables to the temporal evolution of the quantum advantage. This end-to-end system dynamically quantifies the degradation of quantum advantage across diverse turbulence conditions. Our results provide a rigorous theoretical and data-driven pathway for environmental adaptation, facilitating the transition of quantum radar networks from proof-of-principle demonstrations to all-weather operational systems.
summary: This paper addresses the critical issue of atmospheric turbulence degrading Quantum Illumination's advantage in free-space links. The authors introduce a novel physics-driven framework that uses Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks to predict turbulence strength directly from routine meteorological observations. This allows for the dynamic, all-weather quantification of quantum performance, moving QI systems closer to operational reality.
main_problem: The primary challenge is quantifying the degradation of quantum advantage provided by Quantum Illumination (QI) when operating through atmospheric turbulence.
main_result: The authors propose an end-to-end framework that uses deep learning to map macroscopic weather data directly to the temporal evolution of quantum advantage, enabling all-weather operation for quantum radar.
method: They integrate a physics-driven approach using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) trained on meteorological data to predict turbulence parameters ($C_n^2$), which are then fed into the QI channel model.
model_or_system: The system models Quantum Illumination using a two-mode squeezed vacuum state in free-space channels affected by atmospheric turbulence. The framework bridges macroscopic meteorology (T, P, GHI, etc.) to microscopic quantum channel dynamics via KANs.
key_observables: Quantum advantage ($\log_{10} R$), average error probability ($ ar{P}_{	ext{err}}$), and the ratio $R$ comparing classical vs. quantum error probabilities.
important_parameters: Meteorological variables (GHI, $L_\downarrow$, Dew Depression), turbulence structure constant ($C_n^2$), and specific thermodynamic regimes (e.g., twilight, nocturnal boundary layer).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes a physically consistent mapping from standard meteorological variables to quantum channel dynamics, bypassing the need for direct, costly measurements of $C_n^2$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how QI advantage is modulated by GHI (peaking at twilight), collapses under extreme solar forcing or strong mechanical shear in nocturnal conditions, and show the dependence on specific thermodynamic states.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical problem of turbulence degradation for QI. It then details a multi-step methodology: 1) Using MOST/thermodynamics to derive atmospheric parameters; 2) Employing KANs to map macro-weather data to $C_n^2$; and 3) Integrating this prediction into the quantum error probability calculation to quantify advantage.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles the practical deployment challenge of quantum optics by providing a robust, predictive model for environmental noise sources (turbulence), which is crucial for developing real-world quantum sensing networks.
